newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's fate now lies in Tudjman's hands.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's fate now lies in Tudjman's hands.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman, due to be sworn in for another five years on Tuesday, has the power to move his country decisively towards Western Europe in his new term of office.

But diplomats say the 76-year-old Tudjman, who led Croatia through war to independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991, will have to substitute actions for words if he wants to overcome his country's reputation as a laggard in the East European pack.
"Now everything depends on the manner in which Tudjman leads Croatia," a Zagreb-based Western diplomat said. "If his actions meet the rhetoric, Croatia will most likely move in the right direction."

The former Yugoslav army general has until 2002 to tackle some of the issues that have stalled Croatia's stride towards Europe -- improve human rights and democracy, rebuild the war-shattered economy and distribute wealth more equally.
He has already stumbled. In 1995 the Council of Europe postponed Zagreb's bid for membership, citing its poor human rights record and the state control of the media.

Croatia was admitted later but its dreams of joining the European Union and NATO were to suffer further blows. The first round of NATO's enlargement includes only Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland, with Croatia nowhere near.

"Croatia is already behind the curve, way behind many countries, even some in the Balkans - Bulgaria and Romania who have joined Partnership for Peace," a diplomat said, referring to NATO's military cooperation programme.

Visiting British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook rubbed the message in after talks with Tudjman last week. "We want to see Croatia as part of modern Europe, but only if it embraces modern democratic standards."

Tudjman crushed opponents in June's presidential election -- the second in the young country -- proving once again that no rival could seriously challenge his charisma and that he remains a key factor for peace in the volatile Balkans.
Some diplomats, many of them critical of Tudjman's authoritarian rule, believe he will manage to leave behind the years of war and turn to peacetime tasks.

"I am confident in the next five years Croatia will make a big step forward towards the West," another Western diplomat told Reuters. "The outlook is reconstruction, tourists coming in, new highways, agriculture -- the (Croatian government) ministers are preoccupied with economic development."
But prospects depend almost solely on Tudjman as he tries to balance Western demands and nationalist sentiment at home.
There is no sign of an appointed successor to his throne even though U.S. officials said he was treated for cancer late last year. He now looks much healthier and diplomats say he is in full control.
The first victory he is likely to score is the full reintegration of the last Serb-populated enclave of Eastern Slavonia, run by the United Nations until January next year.
The reintegration will work only if he allows Serb refugees in the region to return to their homes elsewhere in Croatia.

Angered by Tudjman's reluctance to encourage their return and by other issues, Western allies, spearheaded by the United States, made the International Monetary Fund and World Bank shut off their financial taps to Croatia this summer.
Yet in his latest meetings with Western officials Tudjman has indicated his readiness to deal with the issues they hold against him.
His hardline rhetoric, delivered to domestic audiences during various tough negotiations, has often been followed by surprise turnarounds along the lines suggested by the West.
"All indications now are that Croatia and Tudjman will live up to the commitments because of (Croatia's) own interests," a diplomat said.
"Unlike Yugoslavia, Croatia is very much responsive because it wants to join the EU and NATO," the first diplomat said. "There may be problems and it will take time, but the outlook is bright."
